summary: One small prefix, בְּ, places an event at a point in time — an hour, a day, a month or a season. At an hour: בְּשָׁעָה חָמֵשׁ “at five o’clock” (also just בְּחָמֵשׁ); on a day: בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי; in a month: בְּמַאי (no article); in a season: בַּקַּיִץ, בַּחֹרֶף (with the article). The other prepositions of time are separate words: לִפְנֵי “before” (and “ago”: לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ), אַחֲרֵי “after”, עַד “until” (מִ… עַד … “from … to …”), מֵאָז “since” (or מִ with a time word: מֵהַבֹּקֶר) and בְּמֶשֶׁךְ “during, for”. As always in Hebrew the noun after them does not change. “Since” goes with the present when the state still lasts — הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר “he has been here since January”, exactly like German seit. A length of time often needs no preposition at all (אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה שָׁעָה), and two days, weeks, months, years or hours have a dual: יוֹמַיִם, שְׁבוּעַיִם, חׇדְשַׁיִם, שְׁנָתַיִם, שְׁעָתַיִם. The clock: הַשָּׁעָה + a feminine number (because שָׁעָה is feminine) — הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ “it is three o’clock”, וָחֵצִי “half past”, וָרֶבַע “quarter past”, רֶבַע לְ… “quarter to”. The date: the day (masculine number, for יוֹם) + בְּ + the month — עֶשְׂרִים בְּמַאי “the 20th of May”. The months are the German ones (יָנוּאָר … דֵּצֶמְבֶּר); next to them lives the Hebrew lunar calendar (תִּשְׁרֵי … אֱלוּל), which fixes the holidays.

blocks.caption: The Hebrew months follow the moon, so they move against the Gregorian ones; a leap year adds a second Adar (אֲדָר א׳, אֲדָר ב׳). Several live on in the Levantine Arabic month names (نِيسَان, تَمُّوز, أَيْلُول, شُبَاط).

blocks.title: Months without, seasons with the article
blocks.text: בְּמַאי, בְּיָנוּאָר (a month is like a name) — but בַּקַּיִץ, בַּחֹרֶף, בָּאָבִיב, בַּסְּתָו (בְּ + הַ fused).

blocks.title: “Since” + present
blocks.text: הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר “he has been here since January”; מֵהַבֹּקֶר אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה “I have been waiting since the morning”. Hebrew uses the present, like German seit; there is no perfect tense.

blocks.title: לִפְנֵי: before and ago
blocks.text: לִפְנֵי הָאֲרוּחָה “before the meal”, but לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ “a week ago” — the same word (and in lesson 12, “in front of”). German vor does all three too.

blocks.title: Dates
blocks.text: Day + בְּ + month, with masculine numbers (the day is a יוֹם): עֶשְׂרִים בְּמַאי, אֶחָד בְּיָנוּאָר. Hebrew-calendar dates are written with letters: ט״ו בִּשְׁבָט (15 Shevat), כ״ט בְּנוֹבֶמְבֶּר.

blocks.title: German and Hebrew side by side
blocks.text: German: um fünf, am Montag, im Mai, im Sommer, vor / nach, bis, seit (+ present!), während. Hebrew: בְּ for the first four, then לִפְנֵי, אַחֲרֵי, עַד, מֵאָז (+ present!), בְּמֶשֶׁךְ — and no cases after any of them. The month names are the German ones (Wiktionary: “from German Januar …”).

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: A point (hour, day, month, season) → בְּ; season with the article.
Before / after / until / since / during → the separate word.
Telling the time → הַשָּׁעָה + feminine number.
Two of a unit → the dual (שְׁבוּעַיִם).

askYourself: Is it a point in time? → בְּ: an hour בְּשָׁעָה חָמֵשׁ, a day בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, a month בְּמַאי (no article), a season בַּקַּיִץ (with the article).
Is it before or after something? → לִפְנֵי / אַחֲרֵי + noun; “ago” → לִפְנֵי + length (לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ).
Until? → עַד; from … to … → מִ… עַד ….
Since? → מֵאָז (or מִ + time word); is the state still going on? → the present.
A whole stretch? → בְּמֶשֶׁךְ, or the length alone (מְחַכֶּה שָׁעָה); two units → the dual.
The clock? → הַשָּׁעָה + feminine number (שָׁלוֹשׁ, שְׁתַּיִם, אַחַת).
A date? → masculine number + בְּ + month: עֶשְׂרִים בְּמַאי.
steps: Decide: a point, a limit (before / after / until / since) or a stretch.
Choose בְּ or the separate word.
For the clock and the date pick the right gender of the number.

traps: *הַשָּׁעָה שְׁלוֹשָׁה → הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ (feminine numbers for the clock).
מֵאָז + present for what still lasts: הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר.
לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ = “a week ago”, not “before a week”.
After בְּ a בגדכפ״ת letter loses its dot: בְּדֵצֶמְבֶּר (bedetsember).

quiz.why: Months take בְּ without the article.
Seasons take בְּ + the article: בַּחֹרֶף, בַּקַּיִץ.
שָׁעָה is feminine, so the clock uses feminine numbers: שָׁלוֹשׁ.
Two units of time form a dual: שְׁבוּעַיִם, יוֹמַיִם, שְׁנָתַיִם.
A state that still lasts takes the present after מֵאָז — like German seit.
לִפְנֵי + a length of time is “ago”.
A date is the day + בְּ + the month.

quiz.q: In which Hebrew-calendar month is Passover?
quiz.why: פֶּסַח is on 15 Nisan (March – April); Tishrei has the New Year, Kislev Hanukkah.

seeAlso.note: Arabic says قَبْلَ “before”, بَعْدَ “after”, حَتَّى / إِلَى “until”, مُنْذُ “since” and في for months and seasons, with the noun in the genitive; Hebrew nouns never change after a preposition.
German um / am / im (+ dative) = Hebrew בְּ; vor = לִפְנֵי (also “ago”), nach = אַחֲרֵי, bis = עַד, seit + present = מֵאָז + present, während = בְּמֶשֶׁךְ.
Chinese puts time words before the verb and uses words after the noun: 吃饭以前 “before eating”, 下班以后 “after work”, 从八点到五点 “from eight to five”.

notes.text: Greek says στις πέντε, τη Δευτέρα, τον Μάιο; Hebrew always uses בְּ: בְּשָׁעָה חָמֵשׁ, בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, בְּמַאי. The clock is built the same way: και μισή ~ וָחֵצִי, και τέταρτο ~ וָרֶבַע, παρά τέταρτο ~ רֶבַע לְ….

Russian takes в + accusative for days (в понедельник) and в + prepositional for months (в мае); Hebrew uses בְּ for all and changes nothing. “Since” + present works as in Russian (он здесь с января ~ הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר). Russian half past three is половина четвёртого “half of the fourth”; Hebrew says שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי.
a las cinco, el lunes, en mayo, en verano — Hebrew uses בְּ for all four. desde + present (está aquí desde enero) works exactly like מֵאָז + present; y media ~ וָחֵצִי, menos cuarto ~ רֶבַע לְ….
English at / on / in are all בְּ; “since” takes the present, not the perfect: “he has been here since January” = הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר. “Ago” is לִפְנֵי + time, in front: לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ.
à cinq heures, lundi, en mai, en été → בְּ for all; depuis + present (il est là depuis janvier) is exactly מֵאָז + present; et demie ~ וָחֵצִי, moins le quart ~ רֶבַע לְ….

um, am, im all become בְּ; seit + present is the same rule (er ist seit Januar hier ~ הוּא פֹּה מֵאָז יָנוּאָר), and vor is both “before” and “ago”, like לִפְנֵי. But halb vier is half past three — Hebrew says שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי “three and a half”.

Hindi puts a postposition after the time word (पाँच बजे, सोमवार को, मई में); Hebrew puts בְּ in front: בְּחָמֵשׁ, בְּיוֹם שֵׁנִי, בְּמַאי. Beside the Gregorian months Hindi speakers use the Hindu lunisolar calendar, as Hebrew speakers use the Hebrew one.
Iran’s official calendar is the solar Hijri one; in Israel daily life runs on the Gregorian months (יָנוּאָר …), and the Hebrew lunisolar calendar fixes the holidays.

Marathi speakers use the Gregorian months beside the Hindu calendar (चैत्र, वैशाख …), much as Hebrew speakers use יָנוּאָר … beside תִּשְׁרֵי …; but Marathi marks the time with an ending, Hebrew with בְּ in front.

Several Hebrew months share their names with the Levantine Arabic months (נִיסָן ~ نِيسَان, תַּמּוּז ~ تَمُّوز, אֱלוּל ~ أَيْلُول, שְׁבָט ~ شُبَاط), all from the old Babylonian names; Arabic مُنْذُ with the present matches מֵאָז + present.

Turkish Şubat, Nisan, Temmuz, Eylül come from the same old names as שְׁבָט, נִיסָן, תַּמּוּז, אֱלוּל — but in Turkish they are fixed Gregorian months, while the Hebrew ones follow the moon and move. Turkish -de / -den / -e kadar ~ בְּ / מִ / עַד.
Japanese numbers its months (五月 “month five”) and puts に after the time (五時に); Hebrew uses names (מַאי) and בְּ before the time: בְּחָמֵשׁ.
Korean numbers the months (오월 “month five”) and puts 에 after the time (다섯 시에); Hebrew uses month names and בְּ before the time: בְּחָמֵשׁ, בְּמַאי.
Finnish uses case endings for time (maanantaina, toukokuussa, kesällä); Hebrew uses בְּ before an unchanged word. And puoli neljä is half past three — Hebrew says שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי “three and a half”.
Hungarian fél négy is half past three — Hebrew says שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי “three and a half”. Time takes suffixes in Hungarian (ötkor, hétfőn, májusban), בְּ in Hebrew.
Swahili time counts from sunrise (saa moja “hour one” = 7 a.m.); Hebrew counts from midnight, like the international clock: הַשָּׁעָה שֶׁבַע = 7 o’clock.
Chinese numbers the months (五月) and puts time words before the verb without a preposition (五点去); Hebrew uses month names and בְּ: בְּחָמֵשׁ, בְּמַאי. 三点半 “three-half” matches שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי.
Vietnamese numbers the months (tháng năm “month five”); Hebrew names them (מַאי). The clock is alike: ba giờ rưỡi ~ שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי.
Inuktitut uses the same locative ending for “at a place” and “at a time” (ullumi “today”, from ullu “day”); Hebrew likewise uses בְּ for both: בַּבַּיִת, בַּבֹּקֶר.
